newsitem.title: CHINA: Underlying weakness troubles China economic growth.
newsitem.headline: Underlying weakness troubles China economic growth.

text.p: Economic tsar Vice Premier Zhu Rongji should be basking this summer after China announced strong first-half growth, offering him a chance to tackle a string of outstanding problems, economists said on Wednesday.
"This set of figures will make Zhu and his colleagues feel very comfortable," said Qu Hongbin, a Hong Kong-based economist with Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
"This is a slower but more sustainable growth rate."
China's economy surged 9.5 percent in the first half of this year, official figures showed. That compared with 9.8 percent for the year-ago period and similar growth for all of 1996.

Economists said this rapid growth rate, coupled with falling inflation and strong exports and without signs of overheating, offered Zhu an almost unprecedented opportunity to tackle tough -- and so far unpalatable -- reforms to what was left of China's lumbering centrally-planned sector.
"He can use this time when inflation is lower and social tension is relatively eased to deliver progress on structural reforms," Qu said.
The problems Zhu must tackle remain numerous, even after he has cooled inflation, forced economic growth down to single digits and imposed some level of financial order.

Steady growth in the first two quarters masked a wealth of difficulties such as slower investment, inflexible interest rates, slack consumer demand, widening income disparities and the perennial poor performance of state firms, economists said.

Losses of state firms running in the red rose 9.2 percent in the half to 67.4 billion yuan. Many have failed to adjust to market pressures as China transforms itself from a Stalinist backwater to a fledgling economic powerhouse.
Much of this year's boom was based on surging exports -- accounting for about two percent of growth.

But the high export growth may not be sustainable, resulting partly from a low base rate after a slump early last year and from a deflationary situation after the credit squeeze of the last three years pushed down output prices, said Charles Li, chief economist with Natwest Markets HK.
Economists voiced concern about the slower growth in fixed asset investment, up by 13.5 percent in the first half but with the rate of increase falling 5.1 percentage points.
"China's economy is traditionally more sensitive to investment injections," Li said, adding that the level could be a factor in second-half growth.
An economist with the State Council, or cabinet, described the growth rate as high and said he did not expect the rate to dip below 7.5-8.0 percent even if investment and demand failed to revive.
"This can't be described as a low growth rate," he said.

At a time when low inflation and the lower cost of subsidies would enable the state to support higher unemployment, Natwest's Li said he expected China to push mergers, bankruptcies and sell-offs of inefficient small and medium-sized state firms.
China is reluctant to give a real unemployment rate, saying urban joblessness hovers at 3.0 percent. It does not include those effectively laid off from state firms in that figure.

One Western diplomat said that while China could find solutions to most of its economic problems, the most urgent issue and one that could destabilise the system by triggering unrest was the rapidly widening gap between rich and poor.
"The strong macro-economy disguises a lot of problems," the diplomat said. "Income disparities are a long term problem...directly linked to social problems."
Latest figures show urban per capita income in the first half rose by just 2.2 percent after inflation, the smallest increase in at least five years.
"High GDP (gross domestic product) growth masks low growth in some areas and high growth in others. It differs province by province. Is the gap closing?" the diplomat said.
